st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source concerns Legal Services Corporation appropriations, recipient audits, funding restrictions and board governance. It does not address legal AI’s task-level capabilities, selective deployment, human verification or workflow redesign, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Legal aid: Funding determines institutional capacity
st.an: The source supplies concrete legislative detail that materially develops the cluster’s institutional-capacity framing: it distinguishes enacted FY2026 funding from competing proposals and shows that appropriations shape capacity through both allocation levels and continuing grant restrictions. It does not independently establish the scale of unmet civil legal need or the effects of funding changes.

st.t: LSC funding: Preservation came with reduced resources
st.an: The compilation directly substantiates the cluster’s core account: Congress preserved LSC at $540 million for FY2026, below the $560 million FY2025 level, while continuing longstanding statutory restrictions. It also distinguishes the enacted amount from the much lower House proposal and higher Senate proposal.

kp.k: Appropriations impose continuing conditions on publicly funded legal aid
kp.d: This compilation concerns legal aid funding and regulation rather than AI. It explains that LSC and its grants are governed by the LSC Act and annual appropriations, with current appropriations incorporating most FY 1996 restrictions through FY 1998 legislation, subject to subsequent modifications. The page distinguishes its convenience compilation from official public laws.
qs: LSC and LSC grants are subject to requirements and restrictions in the [LSC Act](/node/74) and the annual LSC appropriation.

LSC's current appropriation incorporates most provisions of the FY 1996 appropriation through the FY 1998 appropriation subject to modifications in the FY 1998 appropriation and other laws, as indicated in the text.

kp.k: FY 2026 appropriates $540 million across specified programs
kp.d: The reproduced FY 2026 appropriation provides $540 million: $496.3 million for basic field programs and independent audits, $6 million for the Inspector General, $26.2 million for management and grants oversight, $4.75 million each for client self-help and information technology and the Pro Bono Innovation Fund, and $2 million for loan repayment assistance. It requires payment in full at the beginning of the fiscal year. The technology allocation is not described as AI funding.
qs: For payment to the Legal Services Corporation to carry out the purposes of the Legal Services Corporation Act of 1974, $540,000,000, of which
$496,300,000 is for basic field programs and required independent audits;
$4,750,000 is for client self-help and information technology;
$4,750,000 is for a Pro Bono Innovation Fund;
Requires payment of the full appropriation to LSC at the beginning of the fiscal year.

kp.k: Enacted funding differs from congressional committee recommendations
kp.d: The compilation records regular appropriations of $560 million for FY 2023 and FY 2024, with FY 2025 extending FY 2024 funding unchanged. For FY 2026, the House committee recommended $300 million and the Senate committee recommended $566 million, whereas the final agreement provided $540 million. These are distinct legislative stages, not competing measurements of enacted funding.
qs: Extending the FY 2024 Commerce, Justice, Science appropriation including LSC through FY 2025 without changes to LSC funding.
The Committee recommends $300,000,000 for the Legal Services Corporation (LSC), which is $260,000,000 below fiscal year 2025 and $279,000,000 above the OMB Budget request.
The Committee's recommendation provides $566,000,000 for payment to Legal Services Corporation [LSC].
The agreement includes $540,000,000 for the Legal Services Corporation (LSC).

kp.k: Grantee boards can operate with one-third attorney membership
kp.d: FY 2024 provisions, continued in FY 2025, permit governing bodies with at least 33 percent qualifying attorneys without bar-association appointment. The FY 2026 text amends the incorporated FY 1996 and FY 1998 provisions to establish the 33 percent requirement. The Senate report predicts particular benefits for rural recipients and greater inclusion of fiscal experts and community representatives; these are legislative rationales, not measured outcomes.
qs: The bill includes language permitting LSC grantees to operate with boards of directors composed of no less than 33 percent attorneys without requiring appointment by bar associations.
LSC recipients operating in rural areas, where there are not as many attorneys available or willing to serve on boards, stand to benefit most from the flexibility that this provision provides.
This provision also improves the ability of LSC recipients to have fiscal experts, community representatives, and others with diverse skills and perspectives on their governing bodies.

kp.k: Basic field funding combines poverty allocation and competitive selection
kp.d: The incorporated framework allocates basic field resources geographically by the number of individuals in poverty, with specified adjustments and protection for Native American communities' funding share. Competitive selection assesses applicants' understanding of eligible clients' needs, delivery plans, and prior compliance. Previous recipients receive no preference merely because they held an award.
qs: The Corporation shall define geographic areas and make the funds available for each geographic area on a per capita basis relative to the number of individuals in poverty determined by the Bureau of the Census to be within the geographic area, except as provided in paragraph (2)(B).
the quality, feasibility, and cost effectiveness of a plan submitted by an applicant for the delivery of legal assistance to the eligible clients to be served;

No person or entity that was previously awarded a grant or contract by the Legal Services Corporation for the provision of legal assistance may be given any preference in the competitive selection process.

kp.k: Restrictions constrain representation and systemic advocacy
kp.d: The reproduced FY 1996 framework conditions assistance on recipient conduct, including prohibitions concerning redistricting, class actions, specified legislative and regulatory influence, abortion litigation, and litigation for incarcerated people. It also restricts welfare reform activities while preserving individual eligible clients' pursuit of specific relief. The compilation identifies the later invalidation and removal of language limiting challenges to existing welfare law, and separately notes that the attorneys' fees restriction was lifted in FY 2010.

kp.k: Non-LSC funding remains subject to restrictions and exceptions
kp.d: The framework requires recipients accepting outside funds to notify funders that prohibited purposes remain restricted. It nevertheless specifies exceptions or permissions, including use of tribal funds for their designated purposes, non-LSC-funded communications about recipient funding with state or local bodies, and non-LSC-funded public rulemaking comments or responses to unsolicited written governmental requests. Outside funding is therefore not presented as an unrestricted alternative funding channel.
qs: The Legal Services Corporation shall not accept any non-Federal funds, and no recipient shall accept funds from any source other than the Corporation, unless the Corporation or the recipient, as the case may be, notifies in writing the source of the funds that the funds may not be expended for any purpose prohibited by the Legal Services Corporation Act or this title.

kp.k: Noncitizen eligibility contains status-based and victim-related exceptions
kp.d: The statutory compilation restricts noncitizen representation but lists qualifying categories, including permanent residents, certain relatives of citizens seeking adjustment, refugees and people granted asylum, and specified workers. Agricultural workers' eligibility covers designated employment-related matters, while a later amendment includes H-2B forestry workers. The annotated FY 1998 provisions incorporate later victim-related exceptions involving battery, extreme cruelty, sexual assault, trafficking and qualifying immigration relief, and direct readers to additional permissions in 45 C.F.R. Part 1626.

kp.k: Domestic violence eligibility excludes jointly held assets
kp.d: FY 1998 section 506 directs recipients determining financial eligibility for a domestic violence victim to consider only that individual's income and assets, excluding jointly held assets. The conference report frames this as clarification intended to address access concerns, while explaining that comparable determinations were already possible and should not be precluded in other cases.
qs: shall consider only the assets and income of the individual, and shall not include any jointly held assets.
However, given concerns regarding access to the legal system for victims of domestic violence, the conferees have included this provision to provide greater clarity regarding this matter.

kp.k: Recipients must document priorities, time and separate funding
kp.d: The incorporated provisions require nonprofit boards to set written case priorities, staff agreements to follow those priorities subject to defined emergencies, and reporting of matters outside them. Recipients must maintain case-level time records and account separately for outside funds, including Interest on Lawyers Trust Account funds. These are legal aid oversight requirements, not evidence of hourly client billing.

kp.k: Audits and enforcement monitor recipient compliance
kp.d: FY 1998 continues annual recipient audits under the FY 1996 framework. Audits examine financial statements, controls and compliance across funding sources; recipients must report auditor-found noncompliance to the Inspector General within five business days. Enforcement includes withholding or suspending funding for unacceptable audits, grant termination and renewed competition following notice and an opportunity to be heard, and debarment for good cause after notice and an opportunity for a hearing.
qs: An annual audit of each person or entity receiving financial assistance from the Legal Services Corporation under this Act shall be conducted during fiscal year 1998 in accordance with the requirements referred to in subsection (a).

The recipient shall report in writing any noncompliance found by the auditor during the audit under this section within 5 business days to the Office of the Inspector General and shall provide a copy of the report simultaneously to the auditor.
The Legal Services Corporation may debar a recipient, on a showing of good cause, from receiving an additional award of financial assistance from the Corporation.

kp.k: Case disclosure requirements include privacy and safety protections
kp.d: FY 1998 requires basic field programs to disclose specified information about court cases to the public upon request and to LSC in semiannual reports. Party names and addresses are subject to exceptions for legal protections and risk of physical harm. Separately, audit access covers financial, time, retainer, trust-fund and eligibility records and client names, but excludes privileged records; LSC's onward disclosure is limited to specified officials.

kp.k: Disaster supplemental funding targets 2022 extreme weather consequences
kp.d: The FY 2023 disaster supplemental provides an additional $20 million for consequences of hurricanes, flooding, wildfires and other extreme weather occurring in calendar year 2022, available until September 30, 2023. Its operative text generally incorporates FY 1998 conditions but expressly excludes FY 1996 sections 501 and 503 for this supplemental amount, a qualification beyond the overview's general description.
